It ranks the sites from most to least suitable based on mission requirements, allows users to compare locations side by side, discover Earth analogs for recommended sites, and generate a mission report to support informed decisions.
summary:
Stathmos — Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Stathmos is a lunar landing-site research and decision-support application designed to help users identify suitable landing locations on the Moon based on their mission requirements. Users can enter basic mission details, including their planned arrival time, landing window, mission duration and objectives, to explore how different lunar sites may experience sunlight and Earth visibility during their mission.

Rather than simply displaying lunar locations, Stathmos analyses and ranks candidate sites from most to least suitable, helping users understand which locations best match their requirements. Its Site Comparison feature allows users to examine individual sites side by side and make informed decisions. Users can also explore Earth-based analog locations corresponding to recommended lunar sites and generate a Mission Report summarising their findings.

By bringing lunar site exploration, comparative analysis and mission planning together in one platform, Stathmos aims to make complex lunar mission considerations more accessible and support better-informed decisions for future lunar exploration.
details:
What it does :

Stathmos helps mission planners choose where to land on the Moon. You enter your mission once: landing date and time, landing window, mission length (up to 60 days) and objective (geological research, rover exploration, resource investigation, instrument testing, astronaut operations, habitat preparation or other). Stathmos then evaluates all 9,087 officially named places on the Moon and ranks the 8,963 that are not near the poles. Each site gets a mission-specific suitability score with a plain-language explanation. You can compare up to four sites side by side, find similar places on Earth to train and test, and produce a printable mission report.

How it works :

The Moon's day and night each last about two weeks, so the best landing site depends on the exact dates. For every site, Stathmos uses NASA JPL Horizons positions to check where the Sun and Earth are in the sky hour by hour across the whole mission. It compares them with the site's own skyline of hills and crater walls, built from NASA's LRO laser altimeter (LOLA) height map. That gives how much of the mission each site has sunlight for power and Earth in view for radio contact. The score also includes terrain safety (slope and roughness), geology (USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon) and resources: hydrogen as a sign of water, plus iron, titanium and thorium from NASA's Lunar Prospector. Each objective weighs these factors differently. Sites with the Sun up at landing and both the Sun and Earth visible for at least half the mission rank first. The Earth Analogs page compares each Moon site with 196 USGS analog sites, using crater data from a peer-reviewed review of Earth's impact craters, and can search near any city, region or country.

Benefits and impact :

Information normally spread across many NASA and USGS datasets is brought together in one free, offline-capable web page. Students, educators and early-stage mission teams can see why a site suits a mission and how the choice changes with the date. Every value is labelled as real, derived or cached. Missing data is left out, never invented, and the app's own scoring choices are clearly marked as its model, not NASA guidance.

Creativity :

Stathmos turns a complex planning problem into a guided, visual experience: lunar-phase choices, ranked site cards with score dials, a Moon-site picker shown as moons on an orbit, and a similarity score linking each lunar site to real places on Earth.

Tools used :

The web app is a single HTML file written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no server needed. The data-processing and checking scripts were written in Python, and testing used Google Chrome. Data comes from NASA JPL Horizons, NASA LRO LOLA, NASA Lunar Prospector, the USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, USGS geologic and analog-site datasets, Osinski et al. (2022), Lawrence et al. (2022) and Natural Earth. AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) was used to help write the code, the data-processing scripts and text, under the author's direction. No hardware was used.

Factors considered :

Scientific honesty, so nothing is guessed. Lunar day and night cycles over the whole mission. Shadows from surrounding terrain. Landing safety limits. Different needs for different mission types. Accessibility on phones and with a keyboard. Working without an internet connection. Independent checks: the derived values were re-computed and matched exactly.
